lessonRef.subject: ready-for-life
lessonRef.unitTitle: Kitchen Care and Basic Food Safety
lessonRef.title: Application or project: safe tool identification

objective: With an adult, learners examine a set of at least six real kitchen tools and correctly identify which are safe for independent use, which require adult supervision, and which are adult-only, explaining the reasoning for each category.
scenario: With a trusted adult, the learner lays out at least six real kitchen tools — a mix that should include something clearly safe for independent use (a mixing spoon), something that needs supervision (a vegetable peeler), and something adult-only (a chef's knife) — and sorts each tool into one of the three categories before the adult confirms.
safetyNotes: A trusted adult is present for the entire sorting activity.
The learner handles adult-only tools only to look at them, with the adult holding or guiding, never using them unsupervised.

simulationAlternative.description: If six real kitchen tools with adult supervision aren't available together, the learner instead sorts six tools shown in a printed or hand-drawn kitchen-tool set into the same three categories and explains their reasoning in writing, which the adult reviews and confirms afterward.

materials: at least six real kitchen tools spanning the three safety categories

tasks.directions: Before sorting, name one kitchen tool you're already sure is safe for you to use alone, and one you're sure is adult-only.
With your adult, lay out at least six kitchen tools and sort each into: safe alone, needs supervision, or adult-only.

prompts.text: Every tool is sorted into exactly one of the three categories.
For each tool, I said out loud one reason for its category (sharp edge, heat, moving parts, etc.).
My adult confirmed or corrected each sort before I moved to the next tool.

tasks.directions: Write a short reference list of your six tools and their categories, in your own words, that you could hand to a younger sibling.

prompts.text: List each tool, its category, and the one-sentence reason.

tasks.directions: Reflect on the hardest tool to categorize.

prompts.text: Pick the one tool that was hardest to categorize. What made its category less obvious than the others?

remediation: If the learner sorts a tool into the wrong category (especially under-estimating risk), reteach by having the adult demonstrate the specific hazard for that exact tool (for example showing how a peeler blade can still cut) before re-sorting just that one tool.
extension: Sort three additional kitchen tools not covered in the original six, applying the same three-category reasoning without adult prompting before the adult confirms.
